1.title: Define what 'ethical' means for a phone
1.intro: Ethical phones aim for fair labour, responsible minerals, repairability and honest claims.
pts: List the claims you could make: conflict-free minerals, fair wages, repairable design, recycled materials, long updates.
Rank each by buyer interest and by how easily you can prove it.
Survey ten buyers: what would you pay extra for, and what would you not believe?
Write the product promise in one line, with only claims you can prove.
Ask each buyer for one example of a claim they stopped trusting and why; write the reason beside the claim.
Decide how each claim could be proved: an audit report, a lab test, a repair-time test or a published parts list.
List the claims you will not make yet, with reasons, so that sales staff do not repeat them.
1.ex: In a teaching survey of ten buyers, 6 chose repairability, 3 chose seven-year updates and 1 chose 'ethical' branding as the top reason to pay extra, so 9 of 10 (90%) favoured features that can be tested. Promise: 'a phone you can repair and update for seven years'.
1.act: Survey ten buyers and write a provable promise.
1.std: Each claim has a proof plan.

2.title: Know product, trade and labour rules
pts: Radio and electrical safety approvals are required before sale in Canada; test with an accredited lab.
Hazardous substances and battery transport have rules.
Import and customs rules and duties apply to parts and finished goods.
Supply-chain due diligence laws on forced labour require records of supplier checks; keep them.
Ask the accredited lab for a written list of tests and how long they take; plan the launch after the certificate date, not before.
Check the carrier's rules for shipping lithium batteries and write the packing method into your procedure.
Ask a customs broker which tariff codes and duties apply to your parts and write the landed cost per part.
2.ex: Row: 'Sell a phone with a radio | federal radio approval | lab test and certificate | before launch | certificate filed'. Row: 'Ship spare batteries by air | transport safety rules and carrier | follow packing and label rules | each shipment | carrier acceptance note'. If a part costs 400 and duty plus freight add 12% (an assumed teaching rate; check the real rate), landed cost = 400 x 1.12 = 448.
2.act: Build a rules table for importing parts and selling in one province.

3.title: Design for repair and long life
3.intro: Design decisions fix cost, weight and repair.
pts: Use screws and connectors, not glue, for battery and screen.
Choose standard ports and modular parts.
Plan software updates for the promised years and who pays.
Write the repair guide before the first sale.
Do a teardown of a phone you own: count screws, glued parts and cable connectors, and time a battery replacement.
Set a repair target in minutes and tools for each common fault: screen, battery and charging port.
Publish a spare-parts price list and check that a repair costs only a fraction of the phone price.
3.ex: A battery swap takes 6 minutes with one screwdriver; the spare battery is listed at 45 and a screen at 120. A battery plus a screen = 45 + 120 = 165, which is 165 / 780 = about 21% of the phone price.
3.act: Write a design brief with a repair-time target and test it on a teardown of any phone.

4.title: Source ethically and check suppliers
pts: Map tiers: assembler, component makers, mineral sources.
Ask for audit reports and visit where possible.
Use third-party mineral tracing schemes where they exist.
Write corrective actions with dates when you find problems.
Ask your assembler for a list of every supplier and sub-supplier, and mark the ones nobody has checked.
Write a short supplier code of conduct (hours, pay, safety, no forced labour) and get it signed before you order.
Score each supplier from 1 to 5 on five items and set a pass mark; a score below the mark means a corrective plan.
4.ex: An audit finds overtime above limits at a supplier; the corrective plan gives 60 days and a re-check. Scores on five items of 4, 3, 5, 2 and 4 total 18 out of 25 = 72%; with a pass mark of 80% (20 points), the supplier needs the plan.
4.act: Build a supplier scorecard for three suppliers.

5.title: Cost the phone and set the price
5.intro: Costs are bill of materials, assembly, certification, software and support.
pts: Bill of materials per phone, plus assembly and freight.
Fixed costs: tooling, certification, software team.
Warranty provision.
Margin and break-even.
List the bill of materials with part, supplier, unit price and quantity; total it and check the sum twice.
Add the warranty provision as a percentage of sales and test its effect on margin.
Compute break-even at three prices to see how sensitive it is.
5.ex: Price 780; cost 520; margin 260 (33%). Fixed cost 1,500,000 per year gives break-even of 1,500,000 / 260 = about 5,800 phones. If parts are 400 of the 520 and rise 15%, cost rises by 60 to 580, margin falls to 200 and break-even becomes 1,500,000 / 200 = 7,500 phones. Teaching figures in CAD.
5.act: Build the cost sheet and a +15% parts-cost case.

6.title: Sell, support and take back
pts: Sell direct and through carriers or retailers.
Support by chat and repair partners.
Offer trade-in and take-back.
Publish a yearly supply-chain report.
Write a support promise: reply within one working day, with repair partners in named cities.
Make a trade-in offer with a fixed value and check the total cost against the margin.
Plan the first 100 sales by channel, with a number for each.
6.ex: Launch to 100 early customers: 60 direct and 40 through retailers. Take-back target 25% in year 2: of 400 phones sold in year 1, 25% = 100 come back, and if each yields parts worth 60, recovery = 100 x 60 = 6,000.
6.act: Plan a launch to 100 early customers.
6.std: Plan has support and take-back steps.

7.title: Handle data, security and greenwashing risk
pts: Secure boot, updates and privacy by default.
Avoid vague green words; use measured claims.
Plan for component shortages.
Prepare a recall plan.
Test the phone for security basics: encrypted storage, signed updates and no hidden tracking.
Check each green claim against a measurement (grams of recycled plastic, share of minerals traced) before it goes in an advert.
Prepare a recall notice template with steps, contact point and timeline.
7.ex: Risk: 'Chip shortage | 4 x 4 | second source and buffer stock | purchasing | monthly'. Score 4 x 4 = 16 of 25. If you build 200 phones a month and want 3 months of cover, buffer stock = 200 x 3 = 600 chips.

8.title: Pilot a small run
pts: Pilot run with early buyers.
Track failure rate and support tickets.
Stop rule: return rate over 8% means fix before the next batch.
Plan the second batch.
Choose 200 early buyers who agree to give feedback and record each serial number.
Log every return and support ticket with its cause and group the causes weekly.
Hold a go/no-go meeting with the stop rule and the figures printed on the table.
8.ex: Return rate 5.5%; proceed. Of 200 phones, 5.5% = 11 returned, under the limit of 8% = 16 phones. If 6 of the 11 were battery connectors, fix that part before batch two.

quiz: Name two ethical phone claims you could prove.
Repairable design and long software support (or documented supplier audits).
What approval does a phone with a radio need?
Federal radio approval from an accredited lab test.
Why write a repair guide early?
Repairability is a design promise that must be tested.
What is a supplier scorecard?
A scored record of supplier checks with evidence and dates.
Why avoid vague green words?
Claims must be measurable and provable.
What is the break-even rule?
Fixed cost divided by margin per phone.
Why plan take-back?
To recover materials and keep the ethical promise.
What triggers a fix in the pilot?
Return rate over 8%.
Why keep audit records?
Supply-chain laws require proof of checks.
Why diversify chip supply?
A shortage can stop production.
